utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, of course. But first of all, I would like to inform you that my client is not present today either. I haven't received any explanation for today. I don't know what the problem is. But we will continue and finish with the witness and then we will see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Bos.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mrs. Bos, first of all I'm going to set up my position with regard to you and your position as a witness. I don't think that you are a privileged witness at all and I don't think you can be such a privileged witness before this Trial Chamber because this isn't provided for by the Statute or by the Rules of this Tribunal. You're a witness here just like anyone else and you will be cross-examined now. So because of the discussions we had here yesterday, this is my position: You have come here to speak the truth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, we did not get your answer. Will you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you, have you spoken to the Prosecution, to my colleagues from the Prosecution since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to specific questions. Ms. Bos, is it correct to say that you don't know who wrote the diary. You have no idea who the author is? You don't know who this person is at all, you personally, is that correct, this alleged diary?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only can say what I have heard, who wrote the diary. But I don't know myself. I have not seen anybody writing this diary, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In your testimony you said that you made the copy correspond to the alleged original; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you were comparing -- I don't know how the interpreters will manage to translate this -- but you said that you compared the copy that we had with the alleged original that the Prosecutor provided yesterday.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I compared. I didn't make a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Compared. Yes. That's my word. [Interpretation] You also said that you didn't find any differences between the so-called original diary and the copy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, does that mean that the handwritten copy which was given to the Prosecution and suggested as evidence here, does that mean that everything in that copy is the same as in the so-called original?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copy I have seen, as far as we have checked it, there are no differences between the copy I have seen and the handwritten diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you say how you compared the so-called original with the copy?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with one of the language assistants, we looked through the original handwritten diary page by page and we looked through the copy page by page, and we compared each page with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you checked on the contents? You checked that the contents were identical?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not read the diary at that moment, but we checked if the beginning and the end of the pages were the same, and if there were visible changes made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But you didn't go into the contents.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Except for one exception, when there was -- page 42 -- between page 42 and between page 47 there are pages missing and we checked if it was still the same story, what was continuing on page 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you can't even confirm here before the Trial Chamber that the records in the diary are in chronological order, from if beginning to the end. There is no chronological sequence. You can't say that there is a chronological sequence, that it starts with one year and progresses to other years.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've noticed that, sir, but I have not gone into the contents of the diary, but I did see that somewhere it was written "1993," somewhere it was written "1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And in places 87 and 88, after 1991 and 1992, did you notice this -- 88.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but that was not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So what was your task, then, if that wasn't your task?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To compare if the original diary, what we had received, had any changes with the copy what we had received. If there were any changes made in the writing between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, but I'm a little confused. How can you establish such a thing if you don't read it?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You look if you can see if there have been made any changes in the writing. It's -- I mean, if there has been something faded out. It could be visible. So that's how I looked at it. But I said yesterday I'm not an expert. So this is -- I only can say what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, I agree, but I'm telling you that you can't make a comparison if you don't read through all the contents and see that one page corresponds to another page. I have to read it. And just a minute ago you said you didn't read through the contents. So I really don't understand what you are checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President. I object to asked and answered. The witness has said yesterday and again today that she went through the document with a language assistant looking for general comparisons if the two versions looked the same, if there were any obvious changes such as things that had been erased or whited out. She's now said several times she has not read the entire diary word for word, so I think that's clear. There's nothing unclear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, maybe it is clear to you but not to the Defence counsel. That's -- I'll let Mr. Krsnik go for a while, since you have -- still have some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. But I would like to ask you not to let my colleague testify all the time instead of objecting. But what I wanted to say is it's not important whether this is clear to me. I'm just trying to clarify matters for you. But matters have to be cleared for me in order for me to present this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you notice that the handwriting was different in the so-called original?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, no. I compared the original diary with the copy, if there were made any changes. So I did not look at the handwritings. I mean, if the handwriting, the so-called changed handwriting was the same in the copy, then that was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In this original -- you call it an original -- but do you personally know that it's the original? And can you say under oath here before this Trial Chamber that that is the ordinal? Did you establish this yourself?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say what I've been told, and I have seen that in this diary somebody wrote with ink, with a pen, in that diary. It didn't look as a copy to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question though. I've noticed that you call it "the original" all the time. But I'm asking you whether you can claim under oath that -- you can personally claim that that booklet is an original. Do you have direct knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me it looks original, so it call it original, because I don't see that it is copied. I can see that somebody wrote in it with pen. And as far as I can see, this is not a copy of something written. So to me it is an original written document. But again, I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you notice that parts had been written with a felt-tip, parts with a pen, parts with a black felt-tip?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen that there was something written with -- you call it felt-tip, a felt-tip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, I'm telling you that there are at least four to five parts that were written in a different way, and some parts were printed, some parts were handwritten. Haven't you noticed this? For example, what was written with a black felt-tip, do you mean to say that the handwriting is exactly the same as the handwriting in the other parts and that it is the same person who wrote the various parts of the diary? Is that what you want to say under oath?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not tasked to see if the whole diary was written by the same person. I was tasked to compare the so-called original diary with the copy what we have hand over, what we have been given, and whether it has been written with different handwritings, it was not my task. And of course I saw that there were some different pens used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us who received that written copy of the alleged diary on the 9th of December, 1998? Did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of September, 1993, it was my colleague Jan Van Hecke, sir.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 1998. Sorry. I think there is -- I received it on the 10th of September -- sorry, my colleague Jan Van Hecke received it on the 10th of September, 1998. At least he submitted it to the Tribunal on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you weren't even the first person to have contact with it. And where is Mr. Jan Van Hecke now, the chief of your investigation team?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not in The Hague, sorry. He has another assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: He testified in open session here. He didn't mention that detail at all.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an answer on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to clarify the transcript. The question was put to the witness the 9th of December, 1998, and then we got confused about the year. You'll see at line 8. And she said the 9th of September, 1993. Then we clarified the date. We went 1993 or 1998. We clarified the year, but it was never clarified that counsel said the 9th of December. And then once it was suggested that it was the 9th of September, we never got the September corrected. We only corrected the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's the 10th of September, 1998. At line 13, at page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right. I'll come back -- that's not the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, you in fact do not personally know how the Prosecution obtained the diary. You know this from the conversation you had had with Mr. Jan Van Hecke; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it from the records of the ICTY, sir. I didn't have a conversation with Mr. Van Hecke. And for the information, it was the 10th of December, 1998, when he received a copy of the handwritten diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My first question: Do you know the name of the person who handed it over to your colleague Van Hecke? You don't know, because you said that you didn't speak about this to him. So in fact, you don't know who provided your colleague with that diary.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the records, he received it from the Bosnian AID. But I don't know the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You've been working at this Tribunal since 1995 -- or rather, for the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Before that, you worked for the Dutch police.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me please: Since 1995, up until today, has the Prosecution been cooperating with the AID in a very close manner and do you know what the AID is? And if you do, could you tell us what AID represents for you.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: AID is the Bosnian authority who is working with or working for the Tribunal on these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: First of all, I want to tell you, Ms. Bos, that I am sorry to hear this, because the AID is not the organ of the Bosnian authorities. It's the organ of the Bosniak entity in the Federation of Bosniaks and Croats. Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And have you also worked with the Croatian Secret Service, as you did -- or as you have with the AID? Have you worked with the Croatian part of the Federation of Bosniaks and Croats?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far there was no reason to do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But why was there no reason?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was no reason, sir. I cannot explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have direct knowledge of the whereabouts of the original before it was provided to your colleague Van Hecke?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And under what circumstances did your colleague Van Hecke find out that the so-called original existed and when did he find this out?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that my colleague Van Hecke found out the original of the so-called -- of the so-called original, sir, so I cannot answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, I took you to be a person with a lot of experience. As a Dutch policeman in Holland, would you have faith in just one source? Wouldn't you check up on this source and try to find other sources that could verify something?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I only did a piece in this part of the investigation, so I cannot give you an answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But as an experienced policewoman, you must have known that the AID was a secret political police of the Bosniak component, both before the Federation and within the Federation. And it is only responsible to the Bosniak representative and to no one else. It doesn't answer to anyone else in the Federation of Bosniaks and Croats. Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to the question, Your Honour, since --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- it's not working. There's no evidence in the record that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Still no mike. Mr. Scott, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot interpret if the mike is not on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, you know, Mr. Scott, the problem is that the interpreters cannot work if --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My mike is not working, Mr. President. I'm sorry. All our microphones -- perhaps to the value -- the benefit of the courtroom, Your Honour, our -- our.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God is great.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't know we were in the Milosevic courtroom. We've been cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you try that mike, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. It's working now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question. It assumes a number of facts not in evidence. Mr. Krsnik has asserted it's a political organisation. There is no facts in the record to support that. He has also asserted that it doesn't answer to anyone else in the Federation of Bosniaks and Croats. There's no facts in the record to support that. I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this is a claim from the Defence side. But anyway, this question is out of the scope of the cross-examination. Try to concentrate on the matter about that diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I have been very focussed, very brief, and I would be grateful if the witness could testify here, not the Prosecutor. My colleague and Ms. Bos have mentioned the BIS [As interpreted]. These questions -- the purpose of these questions are to discredit the witness. These aren't just claims that I have made. This is the truth that has been established by the Dayton Agreement. And why are we losing -- wasting time on things that are well known and why have we wasted a year on discussing whether it's one language or another since these are things that are well known and it's well known that AID is answerable to the Bosniak people -- or rather, to a representative of the Bosniak people alone and this is in accordance with the Dayton Agreement. These are well-known facts. Why are we to waste time on this just because this suits the Prosecution? All I want to do is to establish and to ask Ms. Bos the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Didn't you say yesterday that the original diary was received by the person you call Mr. Pakenham, if it has been recorded correctly in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. [Previous translation continues] ... of that so-called diary is received by my colleague Brett Pakenham.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, do you know how long -- since when the so-called diary has been or was in the hands of the AID? Do you know this or not?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does the AID cooperate with you in the Prosecution on a daily basis and do they have an office of their own in the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. What do you mean do they have an office of their own in the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do they have an office within the Office of the Prosecutor, within the OTP at this Tribunal? Are you aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is a fact which is easy to establish. Tell me, do you have daily contacts with AID secret agents? Do you have a cooperation on a daily basis with them?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How often do you have contacts with them? How often and when do you have contacts with them? Do you call them? Do they call you? What does your cooperation look like?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hardly have contact with them, sir. I only have contact with them when I'm on mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then they help you bring witnesses, bring exhibits of this or that kind; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mainly help me with bringing the witnesses, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Why isn't it the police who would do that? Because it is their job. Why don't you cooperate with the police? AID after all is the Secret Service, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's an answer -- that's a question I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me please: Why did you say and how did you explain when Mr. Scott asked you about FOSS? Do you know when the FOSS was constituted and what is it and it was the FOSS that handed you over that so-called original on the 24th of September of this year and they had it in their hands since 1993, allegedly. How come that it was only this year that they handed it over to you?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. I have to correct you. It was not the FOSS who handed it over to me. It was to my colleague. I have -- I told you already, I don't know since when they have it. And I cannot answer you how come it was only handed over this year to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, why are you then testifying? You have not received the copy. You have not received the original. You don't know anything. What can you tell us then? Why are you here giving the testimony in front of this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've testified about that yesterday, sir. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Last question: Do you personally know -- let me put it this way: How often are you in Sarajevo? If that is a secret, you don't have to tell us. But give us just an approximate figure. Are you in Sarajevo often; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, we're talking about the FOSS, the new agency which was established a month or two months ago. Did they tell you that the director of the AID, his first and the second deputy, are now in prison because of forgery links with the Iranian secret services, that they are being charged with cooperation with the terrorist organisations, and that -- are you aware of that? Did you hear that in Sarajevo? Did the new agency inform you about that, that they even established a terrorist camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, the witness can answer if she knows. But again, I object that it assumes facts not in evidence. Mr. Krsnik continually asserts things, but that doesn't make -- that isn't evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think this area is out of scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all my due respect, we've been listening for a year about the AID as a very respectable helper of this OTP. Today in this testimony we've heard that the AID is everywhere. And now I can't ask about the director of this agency Bakir Alispahic. The OTP have documents, but again they're playing games with me. And the OTP have handed over those documents to other Defence teams who have asked for those documents. These people have been charged with atrocious crimes, as you may know. And a lady who cooperates with the AID should know that. These questions go -- are about discrediting the witness. But if the lady doesn't know that, then I don't have any other questions. I really don't know why she is testifying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware that these people are in prison, that they are being tried for crimes? You are under oath. Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very briefly. I don't believe I'll have any questions about the diary. Concerning the wooden rifle and the Person X, as a experienced Dutch police officer and an investigator at the Tribunal, when you say the identification card of Person X, was there anything about that card that struck you as an experienced police officer or as unusual or suspicious?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, Ms. Bos, is it unfortunately not an unusual event for witnesses and persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina not to want to be involved, not to want to give evidence, not to want to come to The Hague? Is this situation with Person X unique in your experience?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not unique. I've spoken with several -- several witnesses whose testimony did -- they didn't want to testify because of security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question, Mr. President. I believe that they are speculative and they're out of place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. You may proceed. You may move on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you first spoke with Witness PP about the differences -- the potential differences in the rifle that was in the photograph, the first time you saw him and he made those -- expressed his views, that was only on the basis of the photographs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance. I'm going to put part of the statement of PP on the ELMO. It is -- will not show -- I've turned it so that it does not show his name. If you can just put that on the ELMO, please. I think that would be the easiest thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, counsel yesterday indicated, suggested that Witness PP had said that the -- this rifle was absolutely black. I would like you to direct your attention to the statement about the middle of that page. Did the statement -- did the Witness PP say, "Also according to my memory, the colour of the rifle I was given at that time was also dark, the same as at the photo. I remember that the rifle I was given had a kind of black colour"?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. He told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And could I also -- questions were also put to you about the identification -- of when the rifle itself was shown to PP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could have the usher's assistance, please. This is a statement from the 24th of January of this year, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Witness PP say at that time, up toward the top of the statement, "Today, Thursday, 24 January 2002, you show me a piece of wood, resembling a rifle. I recognise this wooden rifle fully as the one I was given by the HVO on the 17th of September, 1993"? Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of the next paragraph, did he also say, "The colour was the same, although I can see that during the years the colour shade deteriorated a bit"?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bos. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I was just wondering why we didn't see a copy of that statement, seeing that it's -- that two different versions have been given to us, Mr. Scott. The impression that we got from cross-examination was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, I think -- I think you're right. I was trying to do it in a very abbreviated fashion. And I agree with you. I think that the way that the statements were presented to the Chamber during cross-examination were dramatically different than the statements themselves. I'm happy to tender a copy of both statements to the Chamber if -- when we could make a further copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think we'd be much assisted by that, thank you. Ms. Bos, can I ask you a question, please. In looking over my notes from November when Witness PP gave evidence, I noted that he was a very big man. Is that your recollection when you met him in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness X described to you how he got the rifle from a man who was bigger than the other prisoners who came over. So for the moment we can draw an inference from that, for the moment. He -- Witness X went on to say to you that PP, or the big man, gave him cigarettes. Did you put this part of the version given to you by X to PP? And if so, did he comment on it?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Witness PP if he knew anything about cigarettes. That's all I asked him. And then he told me the story about the cigarettes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And is that in the statement that we're going to see?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in the statement you're going to see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And seeing that nobody has brought up the issue of the cigarettes, did he confirm or reject that aspect of X's evidence?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He confirmed that he gave cigarettes to the ABiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think everybody can see why it's so important that we should now see these statements. We've been acting with blinkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, I -- if it was my shortcoming, I apologise. I kept thinking during the cross-examination that they would be shown to the witness, be put to the witness, and they never were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, seeing that you are the person who's been tasked with bringing the wooden rifle to the Tribunal and you've spoken to Witness X, did you ever have an opportunity to look at photographs that were furnished to the Tribunal earlier this year in relation to another wooden rifle?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about other photos, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's fair enough. That's something that we have to look at then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Bos, we're talking about the statements given by PP to you personally. My question to you is as follows: Did they give you personally any statements that they then signed, or are there any such statements or not at all?

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witness PP gave me a signed -- actually, he gave me two signed statements, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you compile these statements and then he signed them? Which statements are you implying? The ones that have been provided to you or some other statements? How were these statements compiled? Are these his statements, or are those excerpts or compilations from your notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're doing it again. You're now making reference to statements that no one in the courtroom can be clear or the witness can be clear. Can Mr. Par please show the statements to the witness so she can make a proper response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, I think, you know, this has to be cleared up a little bit because it's very confusing. We mentioned two statements, and the -- frankly speaking, we don't know what you are talking about, Mr. Par. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be more specific, Mr. President. In front of me I have two statements -- we're talking about Witness PP -- the first one was given on the 29th November 2001. The statement which was taken by Ms. Bos. And the other statement was taken on 24 January 2002, again by Ms. Bos. And my question to Ms. Bos is as follows:

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Are these statements given by the witness or were they compiled from the notes that you made and then the witness just signed them after you compiled them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I'm not expecting to answer this question for Ms. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask the question, Your Honour. I don't understand counsel's reluctance to put the paper in front of the witness. I don't understand that. Now, I have the two copies right here. I ask that they be marked for identification, please be given numbers, and be put in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is one dated the 22nd of November, 2001, and one -- which will be number 4, Madam Registrar. And one dated the 24th of January, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your mike, please. Your mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me, I am continually amazed at how the rules in this Trial Chamber change. Yesterday we requested that statements of AF -- Witness AF be admitted into evidence because in 1996 he gave an extensive statement to AID, he never mentioned Mr. Naletilic, and this Trial Chamber said no, we're not admitting statements. This is our rules. Today Judge Clark invites the Prosecutor to give statements into evidence. I don't understand this. I don't understand this. And by the way, one other thing, Your Honours: The question by Mr. Par does not entail the statement having to be shown to this witness. She can answer the question, did she compile it or did he write it? A very simple question. Mr. Scott wants these statements into evidence. Yesterday we asked to have statements of AF put into evidence and they were rejected. I want -- I just want to know the rules. They keep changing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I think you and I both know the difference between seeing something and putting it into evidence. I want to see, because I feel quite frankly that this Court has been misled. I'm not putting a tooth in it. It is not open to counsel to mislead the Court. We were given a certain impression of a state of affairs yesterday which does not exist. I am disappointed. I now want to see those statements. I think the -- the Bench wants to see those statements. There is a difference between seeing statements which have frankly been mis -- the contents of which have been misrepresented to this Bench and admitting them into evidence. Statements do not prove anything. We just want to see what the contents of those statements are which we're entitled to do at any stage, and especially when the statement has been presented in such a way that the kindest thing I can say is that there has been huge economy with the truth of the contents. That does not mean that what is in the statement proves the truth. But we are now talking about the contents as presented yesterday. Mr. Meek, you and I are long enough in this game to know precisely what the rules are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, do you have an extra copy of your statement? If you have it, please give it to the witness. Do we use Mr. Scott's copy of that statement to show it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I have the statements here, and it makes no difference to me which of the copies are going to be used. And as for the remarks by Her Honour Clark, I must say that I'm very surprised that -- I don't know whether I have understood you well -- that somebody is trying to say that the Defence has been hiding something with regard to these statements. It is in our best interests for the Bench to read this, and I would like everybody to read this. I would like this to be interpreted very slowly, because we are basing our Defence on this. We want -- we are saying that the -- in the first statement this witness said that the rifle was different, and in the second statement he adjusts his statement. So it is our position that you should read these two integral statements because this is one of the elements of our defence. So my question about the statements to the witness was as follows: Whether these statements were written by the witnesses, whether the Witness PP wrote these statements, or whether they were compiled from the notes. I wanted to ask her whether X wrote a statement or whether his words were just noted, and then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then the statement was compiled subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, shall we hear the answer from the witness first? We are not going to prolong the debate of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not want to prolong the debate. This is a matter of -- a procedural matter. Change the rule and allow us to tender these two exhibits into evidence. We are talking about a procedural matter at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We haven't come to that stage yet. Witness, will you please answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I see one statement in front of me which is taken on the 22nd of November, 2001, taken -- I will explain to you how I took this statement. He was with me in the room when I kind out what he told me. It was read over by the interpreter in my presence, of course in his presence. And when he agreed with it, he signed it in my presence and the interpreter signed it and myself, I signed it. The second statement was taken on the 24th of January, 2002. He was with me in the office, where I took the statement. I wrote down in the computer immediately what he told me. No notes were taken, nor from the other one. After I finished with it, I had it read over to him in his own language by the interpreter. When he agreed upon it, he signed it, the interpreter signed it, and myself signed it. And that is about the two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with regard to Judge Clark's words, I'm now asking the Honourable Chamber: Is there a need for us to present the contents of these statements so as to avoid the ambiguities? Do I now start discussing the contents of these statements, or do you now have any suggestion as to how we can establish the exact contents of these two statements? I'm kindly asking for your suggestion as to how we should proceed with regard to the contents of these two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First, I've been sitting quietly, unusually, Mr. President. I don't know about the practices in Croatia. Certainly Mr. Meek knows, and I'm sure Judge Clark knows, any document or item that's used in the courtroom should be marked for identification purposes and for purposes of the record so that the record can be clear six months from now, a year from now, just what it is that's been referred to. The fact that something is given a number does not mean it's admitted into evidence. The rules haven't changed. I haven't offered them. All I asked was that a number be given for identification purposes. The rules have not changed. Having said that, if counsel -- if the Defence now wants to put these two statements into evidence on their initiative, and given the comment that is the Chamber has made, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you are right that we'll give the ID number, an ID number to those two documents so that we could trace it at a later stage. But as for whether they will be admitted into evidence, I think we will discuss it at a later stage. Mr. Par, you may ask some questions concerning the contents of those two documents to this witness to see what the answer is. I'll give the floor to Madam Registrar first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first -- the November 22nd, 2001 statement is ID number 7; and the January 24th, 2002 statement will be ID number 8, under seal, both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, would you please look at the statement taken on 22nd November 2001 and can you please look at the page on which it says "Witness statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Since none of us in the courtroom, including myself now, since I've given up my only copy, has a copy, can it be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It can be put on the ELMO. But be careful of the signature of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to ask Ms. Bos to read the relevant parts from both statements, to provide us with the picture of what the witness actually stated in order to avoid ambiguities. If it is easier for everybody for those statements to be delivered, sent to everybody, I don't have anything to ask the witness. I just wanted to present the contents of these two statements to the Chamber. If it is easier for everybody, if these statements were sent to the Chamber and everybody else, then I will proceed in that way. That was my only intention with these two statements and with the presence of Ms. Bos reading them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have it on the ELMO. If you have any questions, you could ask this witness while she's still in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Ms. Bos, the statement given on the 22nd of November, 2001, the witness was Witness PP. Could you please read out the statement to us.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The witness stated to me: "A few days ago, I testified before the Court in The Hague, against the accused Naletilic, Mladen --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, because the interpreters have to interpret into B/C/S. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Against the accused Naletilic, Mladen, aka Tuta and Martinovic, Vinko, aka Stela. I testified about the wooden rifle incident. "You just showed me photos of a rifle. I can see that the rifle on the photo is made of wood. The rifle on the photo is alike the rifle I was given on the 17th of September, 1993, when we had to walk in front of that tank to the front line with the ABiH at the Bulevar. The rifle I was given had a green-coloured belt. It was an original belt from an original military rifle. The belt was attached to the wooden rifle with two nails. One nail at the rifle butt and one at the barrel of the rifle. On the photo I do not see the belt and the nail on the barrel. "It had a cartridge box, the nail for the trigger, and the nails for the visor, like on the photos. The size of the rifle on the photos also resembles the one I was given at that time. According to my memory, except for the missing belt and nail, the rifle on the photos resembles the rifle I was given at that time."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The rifle on the photos resembles the rifle I was given at that time. "Also according to my memory, the colour of the rifle I was given at that time was --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Also according to my memory, the colour of the rifle I was given at that time was also dark, the same as at the photo. I remember that the rifle I was given had a kind of black colour. "I have to tell you that when I arrived at the ABiH soldiers, I was wounded at one leg and left the rifle and the backpack which was full of stones behind on the stairs when I was taken to a doctor. I never saw the rifle any more. "When we were given the rifles, I asked for cigarettes and one of the KB soldiers gave me a packet of cigarettes. As far as I remember, I shared the packet with the ABiH soldiers because they had a shortage of cigarettes. At that time I was dressed in a full camouflage uniform. I did not give away the HVO jacket. I took it home with me. We were with four prisoners and from the four, I had the most of weight at that moment. I was about 10 kilos lighter, as I am now. Two of us were skinny and the third one was also lighter than I was. I did not know any of the ABiH soldiers --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Bos, we are interpreting what you are saying into French, so please could you read this out slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. "Two of us were skinny and the third one was also lighter than I was. I did not know any of the ABiH soldiers who were at the front line. According to my knowledge, they were with four of them when we first met them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The second statement, Ms. Bos, Witness PP, 24th of January, 2002 is the date. Please could you provide this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher or someone to provide the interpreters with a copy.

utterances.speaker: APOLONIA BOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness at that time stated to me: "I am here on my own free will to give a statement to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. I am doing this voluntarily. No one has threatened me or forced me to do so, nor have they offered me any promises. "On the 20th and the 21st of November, 2002 --" but that's a mistake. It should have been 2001 -- "I testified before the international Court in The Hague. I was a protected witness and my pseudonym was --" and that's redacted by myself. "Amongst other subjects, I testified about the wooden rifle incident that happened in Mostar on the 17th of September, 1993. At that time I was detained by the HVO and together with the other prisoners we were used as a human shield and we were given a wooden rifle. Today, Thursday, the 24th of January, 2002, you show me a piece of wood resembling a rifle. I recognise this wooden rifle fully as the one I was given by the HVO on the 17th of September, 1993. "I recognise the screw in the butt. The screw was used to attach the green strap to the rifle. There was a nail at the barrel to attach the other end of the strap to the rifle. I see this nail is also missing. I recognise the shape and the size of the rifle, the other nails that were used for the trigger and the sights. The colour was the same, although I can see that during the years the colour shade deteriorated a bit -- the colour shade deteriorated a bit. I cannot tell you who made this rifle. The rifles given to the other prisoners were the same as I can remember. "The rifle was given to me about one hour before we had to use it. I had the opportunity to have a good look at it. We were ordered to hold the wooden rifle close to our chests. I did, but the strap detached itself from the screw because the screw was rotating like it is doing now. I was ordered by one of the HVO soldiers to hold the rifle properly. I had to attach the strap to the screw again. The strap was around my neck, like you normally carry a rifle. Later when walked, we had to hold the rifle in the hands, like we had it ready for discharge. "On the 22nd of November, 2001, while I was still in The Hague, you showed me several pictures of this rifle. I then already told you that this rifle resembles the wooden rifle we had to carry in Mostar on the 17th of September, 1993. Now I see the real rifle. I recognise it fully as the rifle I was carrying on the 17th of September, 1993. "I have to tell you that I would not recognise the ABiH soldiers any more, who we met at the Bulevar on the 17th of September, 1993, when we escaped to them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's enough, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's enough for me. I think that we -- that both statements have been recorded in the transcript now and no one can now think that we attempted to manipulate the text in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Madam Bos for coming to give your evidence. When Madam Usher pulls down the blinds, she will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage are there any documents to tender? Well -- yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender the wooden rifle itself, which is P962. And if they weren't previously admitted -- off the top of my head, I'm sorry, I'm not sure -- sorry, but the photographs which collectively were P963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the suggestion that the wooden rifle should be tendered into evidence, we object to this and we consider this to be evidence that hasn't been authenticated, at least as far as its source is regarded, and it hasn't been authenticated by a competent witness. We don't consider Ms. Bos to be competent to authenticate the source and to say where this rifle came from. We only think that Person X is competent to do such a thing, and that person is not present here and that person, Person X, did not write a statement with regard to this matter. But Mrs. Bos only spoke about her conversation with Witness X -- with the Person X, so we don't know the sources of this evidence and this evidence has been attempted to be tendered through an incompetent witness. The Witness PP could perhaps authenticate this, but the Witness PP is not here. I don't know why Ms. Bos would be able to cover these two areas with regard to this evidence, and it is our position that this evidence cannot be tendered, admitted. If this Trial Chamber admits this wooden rifle into evidence, we stand by our earlier proposal and the Trial Chamber has rendered a decision with regard to this, and this proposal is to have the wooden rifle subjected to an expert analysis. Why? Because with regard to identifying the colour of the rifle, this has been in dispute -- it's not just a matter of discussing whether it was black or brown but whether the rifle was painted, since witnesses PP and OO, in their statements before this Trial Chamber and in particular Witness OO said that this rifle was a painted one, because he saw it being painted. Similarly, all those four rifles were said to be identical. So I suggest that the wooden rifle be subjected to an expert analysis to determine whether it was painted, to determine what the colour was, to determine the age of the colour, and to determine how old the rifle is, to determine when the rifle was actually manufactured. And furthermore, we need to establish the traces of the -- of the belt, whether there were nails, et cetera. So we suggest an expert analysis that concerns the colour of the rifle and if the Trial Chamber admits this into evidence. But our suggestion is that this should not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about those photos?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the photographs are acceptable, not at all, for a very simple reason: The photographs were supposed to serve as a means of identifying the rifle at an earlier stage, and the witnesses to whom the photographs were shown did not identify them. And at that point we even had a situation in which the Prosecutor had the photograph as evidence and he himself said that he could not tender this into evidence because the witnesses hadn't identified it. So that was the reason given. So the photographs cannot be admitted evidence because no one has confirmed them. Witness Bos said, "I photographed them." Is that all? That hasn't been identified and we object to this in the strongest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the two sets of the evidence, I think, you know, this Chamber has to go through all the transcripts today and reread all those statements made by this witness and then we'll decide it at a later stage. Well, there is 10 minutes or 15 minutes left in this sitting. Is there anything that both parties want to mention? Mr. Krsnik. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to say today that given the witness who is going to be a public witness, Safet Idrizovic, I would like my client to be present when he testifies. Since he hasn't conferred with me today and he hasn't come to a decision when conferring with me with regard to your decision. So if we manage to deal with the issue of this third witness, who is in a position to -- I don't know whether Mr. Prelec is in a position to testify. I'll try to talk to my client through the Registrar. I hope that he'll come tomorrow. But I don't think that we should waste time. If the Prosecution still insist that is Mr. Prelec should testify, I think that he should testify. I think we can proceed with this matter without my client. But we can't proceed with the testimony of Mr. Idrizovic without my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me respond to a couple of things, please, including the objections to the evidence tendered, because I didn't respond to Mr. Par. The Chamber will know that by many accounts this Tribunal has a rather liberal, inclusive approach to evidence. Hearsay is widely accepted, certainly far more than the jurisdiction where I formerly practiced. And some of us may think that's good and some of us may think that's bad. But jurisprudence of this Tribunal nonetheless is that hearsay is widely accepted. Now, let me put this in context of the Tribunal practice. In some -- if we were to follow what counsel seems to be suggesting, the Prosecution in this case would have had to call a stream of witnesses. I don't know how many witnesses -- to offer one piece of evidence, one piece of evidence. Now, in a pre-trial proceedings, we were continually beaten down. No, Mr. Scott. You can't call more than 50 witnesses. No, you can't call this many witnesses. You must call fewer witnesses. We could have spent 10 witnesses on any single -- whether the rifle or the diary. It could have gone on and on. We think the totality of the evidence at the end of the day between Ms. Bos's testimony, Mr. Idrizovic's testimony, PP's testimony, the testimony that he gave when he was here, when the Chamber puts that all together, there is a sufficient evidentiary basis, we submit, for this evidence to be received and considered by the Chamber and for weight -- for the weight to be given to it as the Chamber deems fit. Now, let me compare this to other cases again. There are other cases, a rather prominent case currently in trial where the Prosecution was told we could only call two witnesses per municipality. For the entire crime base in a municipality, we could call two witnesses. And yet we're being -- it's being suggested here that we're supposed to call witness after witness after witness to authenticate a single exhibit. Let me give another -- cite another situation about hearsay. Again, Mr. President, given the Rules of the Tribunal, this Chamber has received hearsay day after day after day. What if a witness comes in and says, "My brother was at the engineering faculty and he heard Mr. Tuta say --" that's double hearsay. It's not the -- the person who heard it is not testifying. His brother is testifying. And it's directly evidence as to the accused, a statement attributed to the accused, and yet evidence we would receive, I submit, every day. So, Your Honours, the evidence that's been received about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. I can finish, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me hear what Mr. Krsnik wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Scott. Your Honours, Your Honours, why do we have to listen to this? What does this mean? Mr. President, Judge Diarra, we don't come from that system. But I really don't understand these speeches and how can the Prosecutor allow himself to say that he would have found 50 witnesses for the diary, which he showed on the 24th of September? And AID had it in their hands since 1988. Just a moment. I want to finish, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why was it interrupted, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I'm not going to tolerate this any more, put up with you saying you could have found 50 witnesses. If he could have found 50 witnesses, he wouldn't be doing what he is doing now and he wouldn't have received the diary on the 24th of 9. I can't listen to him testifying any more. I can't listen to this hearsay evidence any more, representing hearsay in this manner is a disgrace for the judicial system, wherever this hearsay evidence may be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reason I was on my feet, Your Honours, is because I thought -- I had the right to respond to counsel the arguments that were made on the objections to the tendering of the evidence. I think both sides get to be heard, and I was responding -- making my statement. Mr. Krsnik may or may not agree with it. I'm sure that he doesn't agree with it, but we're stating the Prosecution's position in response to the Defence objection. So we believe, Your Honour, and we respectfully submit that there is sufficient and good basis on the jurisprudence of this Tribunal to receive the evidence that's been tendered, including the testimony of Ms. Bos, and including the hearsay aspects of that testimony. That's our response on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take note of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as to the witness matters that Mr. Krsnik has raised, and I'm responding now to Mr. Krsnik. I've been invited to make a response. Mr. Idrizovic, I won't put too fine a point on this. He's quite unhappy about being here. He's been here all week. We thought he would testify on Tuesday. I completely -- it's highly unfortunate that Mr. Naletilic's health is not always good. We regret that. But Mr. Idrizovic has now been here for a week. He wants to go home. We thought -- honestly told him he would testify on Tuesday, and here it is late morning on Thursday. So that's one consideration. As to Mr. Prelec, Your Honour. I would like to address that with the Chamber. I'm not sure I can -- frankly, I have been meaning for a couple of days to come back to that, and I'm not sure frankly I can do it in the next five minutes. But if the Chamber wishes me to address it now, I try do my best in terms of responding to -- again, counsel has invited me to address the question of Mr. Prelec's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we don't have enough time on that issue. We have four minutes left this sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am in agreement, Mr. President, with that. I do want to be -- I have been meaning for several days, but again I've placed priority - I've placed priority - on hearing the witnesses who have been available. I do want very much to be heard on that issue, on that matter before you end our rebuttal case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, Mr. Par, we don't have time to debate on the admission of the evidence at this stage. You know, the problem is that what witnesses are we going to hear for our next siting? Are you going to comment on that issue? If so, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like us to be granted time to reply to Mr. Scott with regard to his position concerning hearsay evidence. I think that this is a subject that this case depends on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we don't have time, you know, to debate right now. If you have some objections, you are welcome to submit your written submissions to this Chamber. We'll consider it. But now we don't have time to prolong the debate on the admission of the evidence. Right? Let us make a ruling on the next witness we are going to hear. Okay? Well, Mr. Krsnik, I'm very sorry to hear that your client is not in good health. As I said yesterday, that this Trial Chamber cared very much about his health. We wish him a speedy recovery. But on the other hand, we have a witness waiting to testify. Could I give you some time -- maybe two hours of time for you to check with your client whether he's available at 2.30 this afternoon for this afternoon's hearing. I hope -- I hope he could be present at this afternoon's hearing or he could allow us to continue without his presence for just one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, it's not possible to say that this Defence counsel hasn't been cooperative and that we haven't tried to interfere with the schedule. Your Honours, this is the last witness who is important for my client. Once again, I want to emphasise the fact that any delay damages the Defence. We haven't got much time finish our closing brief, because you haven't postponed the time limit. So it's in my interest to finish, as it is in yours to finish, as soon as possible. Your Honours, all I can do with your permission is -- I have to go to the prison. I can't get back before 2.00. If we started at half past 2.00 and continued until 4.00, I think, we could listen to the examination-in-chief from half past 2.00 to 4.00 and then he could be present for the cross-examination tomorrow. He could at least be present for the cross-examination, if he can't be present for the examination-in-chief. This is my suggestion. I think it should be acceptable to everyone. But we could listen to Mr. Prelec up until half past 3.00 if the Prosecutor still insists on this witness testifying now. I don't see why we're wasting time here. My colleague has just suggested that we should either listen to the examination-in-chief and then have the cross-examination tomorrow and then I'll go to prison and speak to my client, to arrange for him to come to the cross-examination tomorrow. So this is a second possibility. Whichever possibility you opt for, it's all the same for me. It's more important for my client to be present during the cross-examination than to be present during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think, you know, we prefer to have that -- you know, to hear that witness on our schedule this afternoon at 2.30. I hope during the lunchtime you could get in touch with your client and at the same time I also instruct the registrar to find out how serious your client's illness is. But anyway, we'll start the direct examination at 2.30 with that witness this afternoon. Having said that, we will resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.01 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we start, is there anything that both parties wants to address? Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to inform you about my contact with my client. Madam Registrar has been there as well. My client has undergone various medical check-ups today, one of them being an EKG. He is not feeling well. He cannot be here today, but he will try to be here tomorrow at any cost, so I would kindly ask you if -- whether he is here tomorrow or whether he is not here tomorrow, let's wait with my cross-examination until tomorrow. If he is not feeling well tomorrow, I have his consent to carry out my cross-examination. So on his behalf I would kindly ask you to permit me not to start with my cross-examination today and tomorrow, even if my client still feels bad, tomorrow I have his consent to do my cross-examination tomorrow. So I would kindly grant your permission for that. So direct examination obviously can take place today without his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. During the long break our client asked me to address the Chamber and for that I would need to go into private session, please, because I have a request to put to you on behalf of my client. But I have to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all -- absolutely all due sympathy for any health conditions being suffered by the two accused, I have -- I find the timing of all this quite interesting. I might as well tell the Chamber now that I beseech the Chamber to let this witness be finished so he can go home. He's been here since last -- it's a week today, and I have a sense - I have a sense - that we're moving in the direction -- we're not going to finish him tomorrow. He's going to be required to stay over a second weekend. He will have been in The Hague for almost two weeks and that is unfair to this witness, and I will -- I'm just telling the Chamber now I'm going to make every effort -- ask the Chamber to make every effort, please, that he can be finished so he can go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll take note of what you said. Mr. Seric, I hope you could file us a motion about the health condition of your client as well as his complaint about visits from his family so that we could, you know, send it to the Registrar, to the warden of the Detention Unit, and ask them to improve it, or some possible medical check-up for your client. Now is the season for changing of the weather, you know. I think, you know, in this building a lot of people, you know, got sick, and all the people are vulnerable at this moment, especially those who have been confined in the -- in the Detention Unit. So your request is permitted, and Mr. Martinovic could go back to the Detention Unit to have a rest. All we wish is that you have a speedy recovery from your suffering. The guards will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Madam Usher, could we have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes. Shall we start direct examination? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Will you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Safet Idrizovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, I think it only fair to say I apologise for the length of time you've been in The Hague, and I also want to advise you the two accused -- because you may find it curious in the courtroom -- the two accused have been excused because of health problems. But nonetheless, your testimony is very important to the Judges. Is it correct, sir, that you are from and grew up in the region of Jablanica in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in what municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: In Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, as I have told you previously some days ago, you are here even though you have a much fuller story that you could tell, for a particularly specific focus. So I'm going to direct your attention right away to some specific items. Directing your attention to the last few months of 1992, did you hold any position or rank in the Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the Muslim armed forces. I was with the municipal staff of Territorial Defence. I was an operative until 28 October 1992. Then by the order of the commander of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina I was appointed the commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence in Jablanica. I discharged those duties until the end of hostilities between the BH army and HVO, that is, the end of January 1994. The end of 1992 or early 1993, from the commander of the 4th Corps, Mr. Pasalic, who was my superior, I received an order to establish a brigade in Jablanica. I did that in the following manner: The majority of the members of the Territorial Defence staff I deployed into that unit. At that time the majority of the units of the BH army were brigades, and the staffs usually existed in those municipalities which were at the time integral, which remained integral, and the brigades had the task to participate in the operations, wherever it was necessary. Since we were in the southern part of the republic, at the time our tasks, the tasks of those brigades, were to block Sarajevo and Gorazde, because these two cities were under the greatest danger, under the greatest threat. Very few officers remained in the municipal staff; mostly the aged ones. When the brigade was established, then we mobilised some older members, and the staff was tasked with guarding facilities in the territory of the municipality. There were very important facilities such as the war hospital, the industrial objects, the hydroelectric power plant and related facilities, refugee camps, warehouses storing humanitarian aid, water pipes, bridges, and all the other facilities, so that on -- between 21st January and the end of the conflict with the HVO, I had that task -- my units were actually charged with that task. After the end of hostilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you. Let's take it in somewhat smaller pieces. I think it's just easier for I everyone. If I can also caution you, please. You probably understand that what you say is being translated -- it has to be translated into English and French. So -- at least it appears to me that you're speaking a bit fast, so if you could slow down just a bit.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, in terms of what you just told us, let me just pick up on a couple of points. After the end of January or as of the end of January 1993, did you have any role in what you've called the brigade, the HVO brigade in the Jablanica area, as opposed to the municipal -- what you've described as the municipal staff?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: It was not an HVO brigade but the BH army brigade. I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, sir. I've been doing this, I think, too long. As of the end of 1993 -- or excuse me, January of 1993, you've discussed that there was a reorganization of the ABiH units. A brigade was formed. And if I heard you correctly, sir -- I just want to be clear -- a brigade was formed and you became responsible for something called the municipal staff, which primarily guarded facilities in the town of Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was never a member of the 44th Mountain Brigade that was established. Only younger members joined that brigade. At the time I was already too old to join that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection, sir, with the 44th Mountain Brigade, the commander of that brigade was a man named Enis Kavacevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he ever your commander after February 1st, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was not my commander. Until January 1993 I was his commander. He was never my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then as part of this reorganization, he went off to become the commander of another unit and the two of you were separate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was your unit, that is, the Jablanica Municipal Staff, involved in any fighting in Konjic in April or May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Municipality Staff only had such units which provided security for various facilities. And it wasn't armed. They didn't have any automatic or semi-automatic weapons. The only weapons he had were just ordinary rifles because all the other weapons were given to the newly established brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was your unit, sir, the Jablanica Municipal Staff, involved in any fighting around the place called Grabovica in early September 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: No. It never participated in any actions. These units were tied exclusively with facilities and their protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, how are you presently employed, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: I work -- I'm affiliated with the hydroelectric power plant on the Neretva. Actually, it is a company that manages three various plants, logistics. I am the head of the security and fire protection there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you also work for this company before the war, that is, for example, in 1990/1991?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for one part of that company, which was much larger before the war. It had five power plants, and I worked in one of its facilities called maintenance.
